note: The Scriptorium's faces and the tree that groups them (docs/inklings-typography.md §6, §7). The taxonomy is Vox-ATypI (Maximilien Vox 1954, adopted by ATypI 1962), PRUNED: Vox's Glyphic and Graphic are grab-bags and Gaelic / Non-Latin are a tail a Latin skeleton can't teach — ATypI itself deprecated the scheme in 2021, partly for that Latin-centrism. This is a teaching simplification and should keep saying so, the way the ladder corpus's rungs do. Every group is a PEN, which is why data/nibs.json and this tree are one body of information seen twice.
capitals: M7 (§10). Every face carries a `caps` paragraph — the plate shows it while an uppercase letter is selected — and `unicase: true` marks a face with no case distinction, whose A and a are one drawing and ONE album cell. Anatomy callouts are keyed by CHARACTER, so a capital-only term is simply a row naming an uppercase letter. A face keeps TWO fractions, 26 minuscules and 26 majuscules, never one of 52: folding them would drop a 100%-complete face to 50% on update and un-fire a milestone that had already paid.
faceNames: Faces carry their REAL font names. §4's pun-a-new-name advice applies only to a face we would have to redraw to ship (Papyrus — the blocker there is the file and the trademark, never the letterforms); everything here is OFL and shipped honestly, and 'Garamond' IS the teaching payload.

groups.name: Classical
groups.note: Faces whose forms still remember a pen.

groups.name: Humanist (Venetian)
groups.tell: the slanted bar on the e

groups.name: Garalde (Aldine)
groups.tell: a horizontal e-bar over an angled stress

groups.name: Transitional (Réale)
groups.tell: sharper, more open forms than a Garalde

groups.name: Lineal (sans)
groups.note: One pen for the whole branch — a monoline has no stress to vary, so these three leaves are told apart by PROPORTION, not by tool.

groups.name: Grotesque
groups.tell: monoline, closed apertures, a slight optical contrast

groups.name: Script
groups.tell: entry and exit strokes that want to connect

groups.name: The bare hand
groups.tell: no tool at all — the skeleton itself

faces.name: The Bare Hand
faces.origin: the alphabet as a set of bones, before any pen touched it
faces.plate: The face you start with, and the only one whose specimen is not a font: it is the shared skeleton (data/wordshape-alphabet.json) drawn with the round pen. Everything else in the album is this same skeleton wearing a tool.
faces.caps: The capitals are the same bones under the same round pen — but they were never a pen's alphabet at all. A Roman capital was laid out with a flat brush and cut with a chisel some eight hundred years before the minuscule existed, which is why it is not a big lowercase: it stops short of the ascender at cap height, and its widths are a SYSTEM. O and Q are circles, E F L B P S are narrow, M and W are wide, I is a stem. You can read that in a book; you can only feel it by travelling it.

anatomy.note: One stroke: the bar left to right, then up and over and round — the way a hand draws it, which is why the skeleton could be traced at all.
The height of the lowercase body. Every face in the album shares this skeleton's x-height, so the differences you see are the pen's.

A capital stands on the baseline and stops BELOW the ascender. Trace an H, then an l: the l overshoots it. Drawing capitals up to the ascender is the most visible possible error there is against a real font.
O is a circle, E is narrow, M is wide — classical proportion is a set of width classes, not one column. Trace O, E and M in a row and you have travelled it.

faces.name: Cardo
faces.origin: David J. Perry, after Nicolas Jenson's Venice
faces.plate: The first roman types cut in Venice copied a humanist scribe's broad pen held steeply, and the giveaway survived into every revival: the bar of the e runs uphill, because a steep pen cannot draw it flat.
faces.caps: Jenson took his capitals off Roman stone, not off a scribe, and set them beside a pen's minuscules. That pairing is what a roman typeface IS — two alphabets from different centuries taught to share a page.

anatomy.note: Draw a line through the two thin points of the o: on a humanist face it leans a long way left of vertical. That angle IS the pen's angle.
The one-glance test for a Venetian face.
Wide and open — the terminals stay far apart.
Not decoration added at the end: it is the flat brush entering and leaving the stroke, and the chisel followed the brush. Trace an E with the flat 0° nib and watch it appear on its own.

faces.name: EB Garamond
faces.date: 2011 revival of types cut in the 1530s–40s
faces.origin: Octavio Pardo, after Claude Garamond, Paris
faces.credit: EB Garamond — Georg Duffner & Octavio Pardo (fonts/EBGaramond-OFL.txt)
faces.plate: The pen has dropped a few degrees from the Venetian angle and the e-bar has come level — but the stress is still angled, and the whole face is still a record of a quill. This is the face most books you have read are descended from.
faces.caps: Garamond's capitals stop a little below his ascenders so a capital never crowds the line above. That small mercy of the Aldine page is exactly why cap height is a metric line of its own and not just the ascender.

anatomy.note: Still leaning, but less than a humanist's: the pen is flatter.
The difference between a Garalde and a Venetian, in one stroke.
The serif joins the stem on a curve, the way a pen leaves a stroke. A nib cannot draw this — it is a finishing gesture, which is why your traced glyph has the right stress and the wrong terminals.

faces.name: Libre Baskerville
faces.origin: Impallari Type, after John Baskerville, Birmingham
faces.credit: Libre Baskerville — Pablo Impallari & Rodrigo Fuenzalida (fonts/LibreBaskerville-OFL.txt)
faces.plate: The hinge of the whole classification. Baskerville's smoother paper and sharper impression let the contrast rise and the stress stand up straight — the broad pen is being abandoned mid-face for the engraver's point.
faces.caps: Baskerville's capitals are wider and more even than a Venetian's, and their stress has turned vertical along with the lowercase — the pen leaving the alphabet, the engraver arriving.

anatomy.note: Nearly vertical now. Compare it against the Garalde's o on the same plate: that rotation is a century of printing technology.
Thick stems, thin bowls — further apart than a Garalde's, not yet a Didone's.

faces.name: Libre Bodoni
faces.origin: Impallari Type, after Giambattista Bodoni, Parma
faces.credit: Libre Bodoni — Pablo Impallari, Rodrigo Fuenzalida & Danilo de Marco (fonts/LibreBodoni-OFL.txt)
faces.plate: The end of the road the Transitional started down: stress dead vertical, horizontals reduced to hairlines, serifs flat and unbracketed. Nothing here remembers a quill — it remembers a burin.
faces.caps: The extreme case: fat vertical stems, hairline flat serifs, and no bracket at all between the two. Trace an E with the flexed pointed nib and watch the arms very nearly disappear.

anatomy.note: The thinnest part of a Didone is thinner than anything a broad nib can produce, which is the argument for the pointed pen in one picture.
The serif meets the stem at a right angle, with no curve easing in.
Bowl thin at top and bottom, thick at the sides — pressure on the downstroke and nowhere else.
The hairline arm meets the fat stem at a right angle with no curve between them. On a garalde that join is a bracket; here it is a corner.

faces.name: Bitter
faces.origin: Sol Matas — a slab serif for screens
faces.plate: Nineteenth-century advertising needed letters that shouted, so the contrast was thrown away and the serifs were fattened into slabs. A slab is a monoline face wearing heavy terminals — which is why its pen here is a round one.
faces.caps: Slab capitals are the Roman width system with the serifs squared off. The widths survive the industrial revolution even where the modelling doesn't.

anatomy.note: A rectangular block, the same weight as the stem. The nib cannot draw this: a later terminal knob will stamp it at the stroke ends.
No stress to find — every part of the bowl is the same width, so there is no axis to draw.

faces.name: Archivo
faces.origin: Omnibus-Type, after the grotesques of Berthold and Stephenson Blake
faces.plate: The first sans serifs were called grotesques because a letter without serifs looked monstrous. They are monoline and a little grudging about it — apertures close up, the terminals cut off horizontally.
faces.caps: A grotesque pulls the classical widths toward each other — its O is no longer a circle and its E is no longer narrow. That evening-out is a good part of why a sans looks like a sans.

anatomy.note: The terminals curl in toward each other. This, not the pen, is what separates the three sans leaves.
Cut flat, at right angles to the stroke.
Set E beside O in this face and then in Cardo. The grotesque has narrowed the O and widened the E toward one shared width.

faces.name: Jost*
faces.origin: Owen Earl, after Jakob Erbar and the Bauhaus turn
faces.plate: A sans built out of the compass and the ruler rather than out of a hand: the o is a circle, the a loses its second storey, and the alphabet stops pretending it was written.
faces.caps: A geometric sans goes the other way and makes the O an actual circle again: Bauhaus arithmetic arriving at the Roman answer from the opposite end.

anatomy.note: As near a true circle as a readable face allows.
A geometric decision, not an italic one — worth knowing before §10's style axis, where a single-storey a is the mark of a TRUE italic.

faces.name: Open Sans
faces.origin: Steve Matteson — an upright humanist sans
faces.plate: Take the proportions of a Garalde — the wide o, the open c, the varying letter widths — and remove every trace of the pen. A humanist sans is a monoline face with a scribe's skeleton, which is exactly what your traced glyph always is.
faces.caps: Humanist sans capitals keep the classical proportions the grotesques flattened — wide O, narrow E — which is most of why they hold up in a long line of text.

anatomy.note: The terminals stay apart, unlike a grotesque's.
Compare the width of e against o: a geometric face would make them nearly equal.

faces.name: UnifrakturMaguntia
faces.origin: j. 'mach' wust, from Peter Wiegel's Berthold Mainzer Fraktur
faces.plate: The same broad pen as a Garalde, held far steeper and lifted more often. At 45° a curve cannot be drawn in one sweep, so it is BROKEN into angled strokes — the black woven page that gave blackletter its name.
faces.caps: Told straight (§10.6): a Textura majuscule is a DIFFERENT ALPHABET. The real ones are bowed and doubled and hung with hairline flourishes, built from nothing like the Roman skeleton. What you trace here is the shared skeleton under a 45° pen, which comes out Lombardic rather than correct. A true blackletter majuscule skeleton is parked beside the true italic — both are a second drawing, and that is the lesson rather than the excuse.

anatomy.note: Not a bowl but four straight strokes. The pen angle made the decision, not the designer.
Thin where travel runs along the nib's edge — at 45° that is the diagonal, so the hairlines run corner to corner.

faces.name: Uncial Antiqua
faces.date: 2011, after uncial hands of the 4th–8th centuries
faces.origin: Tom Murphy 7, after late-Roman and insular book hands
faces.plate: The opposite extreme from blackletter with the same tool: the pen laid almost flat. Horizontals go thick, verticals go thin, and the letters swell into the round majuscule forms of a Gospel book. Uncial is also where the case distinction has not happened yet — these are neither capitals nor lowercase.
faces.caps: Uncial has no case at all. It is older than the split — the majuscule/minuscule distinction was invented after it — so A and a are one letter and one drawing. The pad hands you the single skeleton either way, and the album's two cells are one cell.

anatomy.note: Thin at the sides and thick top and bottom — the reverse of a Didone, from a pen instead of a point.
A flat pen rewards the arc and punishes the corner, so the hand rounds everything.
Pick A and the pad still gives you a. Not a shortcut — uncial predates the two-case alphabet, so there is no capital to draw.

faces.name: Pinyon Script
faces.origin: Sorkin Type, after engraved copperplate hands
faces.credit: Pinyon Script — Sorkin Type / Eben Sorkin (fonts/PinyonScript-OFL.txt)
faces.plate: A pointed flexible pen, never lifted: the same tool as a Didone doing the opposite job. Pressure on the downstroke swells the stem, the release runs out to a hairline, and the hairline carries on into the next letter.
faces.caps: Script capitals are swash: a flourish entering, a flourish leaving, and the letter in between. The pointed nib does most of that work and the shared skeleton gets you a fair engraved capital — but not the swash, which is a flourish and not a letterform.

anatomy.note: Heavy coming down, hairline going up. One stroke, two weights — the pointed pen in a single gesture.

The hairlines that reach out of both sides to join the neighbours. The skeleton has none, so a traced script is the one face that visibly wants something the shared bones cannot give — which is §10's argument that a true italic is a SECOND skeleton.
